newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: NATIVE TITLE GROUP TRAVELS TO EUROPE
A six-person delegation from the National Indigenous Working Group on Native Title flies to Europe today to raise awareness about alleged breaches of human rights in Australia.
Delegation member Aden Ridgeway says of particular concern is the Federal government's response to the Wik decision and the Stolen Generation report.
Another delegate, Olga Havnen, says the Working Group won't be calling for trade sanctions or boycotts by European countries.
Rather, she says they hope to provide European countries with an improved understanding of Native Title and the Federal Governments' Wik response.

Ms Havnen says her group believes many of the Government's proposed amendments to the Native Title Act may be in breach of international law and international standards, specifically, the Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.
She says talking about these issues overseas is a way of gaining a better level of debate about native title.
The group has arranged to speak to human rights committees and European parliamentarians.
HOWARD SAYS CLOTHING INDUSTRY WILL BE TREATED SAME AS CAR
Prime Minister John Howard says textile, clothing and footwear will be treated in the same way as the car industry in deciding tariff levels.
The Productivity Commission has released a draft report recommending tariffs in the textile, clothing and footwear industry fall to 5 per cent by 2008.
Speaking on radio Three-AW in Melbourne, Mr Howard this morning said a decision had not been made and the Government will seek comment on the draft report.

"We'll go through the same procedure with this as we went through with the car industry and that is get people's opinions. And then when we get the final report which will be in a few months we will take a quick decision," he said.
Meanwhile Victorian Premier, Jeff Kennett, says the proposals to slash tariffs on imported clothing, footwear and textiles will only benefit Australia's competitors.
Mr Kennett says if such proposals became policy it would be disastrous.
HOWARD SAYS AUST CAN'T MONITOR HONG KONG
Prime Minister John Howard has rejected suggestions that Australia monitor developments in Hong Kong after the British colony is handed back to China tonight.
Speaking on radio 3AW in Melbourne, Mr Howard this morning distanced Australia's future involvement.

He said Australia couldn't say it was realistic and proper that colonial rule in Asia finish altogether, then think it could continue to exert the same influence as it did when Britain was controlling the territory.
Mr Howard said Britain has the same values, institutions and belief in full-blooded democracy as Australia but will no longer be controlling events in Hong Kong.
He said things were going to be different in Hong Kong and it was unrealistic of any Australian to think otherwise.
BIG INSURANCE PAYOUT TO SA TUNA FARMERS
In South Australia, tuna farmers at Port Lincoln, who lost $60-million worth of fish in violent storms last year, will share in an insurance payout, believed to total about $14-million.
They've reached an out-of-court settlement.
About 60,000 tuna died in Port Lincoln's Boston Bay in April last year.
MMI Insurance initially rejected a claim by 13 tuna farmers for a total of $14.7 million, prompting legal action through the Federal Court, where the parties were directed to negotiate.
Industry representative Brian Jeffriess says the terms of the settlement will remain confidential.
But, he says they'll pursue criticism by some politicians and scientists that the industry was somehow responsible for the losses.
ALICE SPRINGS NATIVE TITLE CLAIM BEGINS
A hearing into a native title claim over parts of Alice Springs begins in the Federal Court in the Central Australian town tomorrow.
Claimants will try to show the court they've had a continuing relationship with the land, despite efforts to sever the link.
Claimants want native title rights mainly over crown land within the town boundaries, including the Todd River bed and at the Telegraph Station.
The Alice Springs Arrente native title claim, will be heard by Justice Olney.
There will be three weeks of evidence, from the older claimants, followed by a week of cross-examination by the Northern Territory Government.
Claimants will be able to give evidence in groups and on visits to sites around the town.
The month-long sitting is just the beginning of the hearing, which is expected to resume in February next year.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
